I am confused by the fact that the new SSIL actually means complete screen space GI. I understand that [this is the original name from the authors of SSIL](https://cdrinmatane.github.io/posts/cgspotlight-slides/), and, iirc, the maintainers also suggested using the existing SSIL field, but I still think this is not the way for Godot, which tries to be simple. What if a user enables SSAO along with the new SSIL and selects SSIL_TYPE_AO or SSIL_TYPE_BOTH? 

I suggest getting rid of the SSILType field and introducing SSAOType (Simple (current ASSAO) and Ground Truth) instead, which will naturally eliminate the non-obvious mechanics above. Btw, this is exactly what the existing PR for the XeGTAO did (see #113304). But tbh idk how much this will change your code... If I'm not mistaken, the current SSIL and SDFGI already share some info to optimize performance.

In that case, the PR may be asked to be split.

And btw, I suggest you clearly state in the PR description that GTAOVB is better than XeGTAO in everything, so #113304 may become irrelevant.

So, I poked around with the PR in Bistro, trying to see what I could get out of it in terms of visual quality. This is the scene I experimented with, rendered in Cycles: This is with only SDFGI in Godot: SDFGI + new SSIL high, mode both, radius 2m, intensity 1.0, thickness 0.5, no backface reject (so default settings): The most evident thing to me is that the PR's SSIL seems to compensate for SDFGI's splotchiness, getting rid of unnaturally dark areas in the image, such as: under the scooter, inside the menu board, and on the sides of the blue-ish shop on the left). Other than that, there's also some soft occlusion under the tables, which is neat and matches the raytraced reference. However, notice that there's also some areas that should have occlusion (see render) but barely have any, such as the window on the yellow wall or the vines on the walls. I tried increasing the SSIL intensity, but this only made everything brighter (yes, it's set to `both`; more on this later). So instead I enabled SSAO, with these results under default SSAO settings: Now we're starting to get some more detailed occlusion. More tweaking: - SSIL: high, both, radius 2.0m, intensity 2.0, thickness 0.5, backface rejection on - SSAO: full res, medium, radius 0.4, intensity 2.0, power 3.0, details 5.0 Things are starting to come together: PR SSIL compensates for SDFGI's splotchiness and provides soft larger-scale AO, while SSAO provides the more detailed AO which SSIL misses. However, there's now occlusion in areas which shouldn't have it. I experimented more and landed on this setup: - SSIL: high, both, radius 2.0m, intensity 2.0, thickness 0.5, backface rejection on - SSAO: full res, medium, radius 0.5, intensity 12.0, power 1.5, details 5.0, horizon 0.7 The occlusion is less aggressive than before, but most importantly now it doesn't occlude areas that shouldn't have occlusion. For comparison, this is what the above looks like with SSIL alone: And SSAO alone: Considering all of this, I believe that the best visual results are obtained when both SSAO and the PR's SSIL are combined. SSIL for fixes to SDFGI's issues and soft large occlusion, and SSAO for details. I'm pointing this out because, and maybe I'm misunderstanding things, but I've gotten the impression from chat discussions that this PR is being seen as a replacemenet for the existing SSAO, on top of replacing SSIL. I don't think that this PR's AO/both mode is a valid replacement for what the existing SSAO does, though it is useful when *combined* with existing SSAO. Now, a few things I noticed. This new SSIL implementation allows to control bounce light intensity independently of AO strength (through `intensity`), and, bug or not, I like that; it allows to more finely adjust lighting, such as to compensate for SDFGI dark spots or to compensate the darkening caused by stronger SSAO values. It's a legit feature. And if it's a bug, then it should be a feature. The existing SSIL's behaviour is to scale both AO and bounce light intensity at once, which completely prevents the really useful kind of SDFGI dark-spot compensation that this SSIL has with its split bounce/AO intensity control. It would also be handy to have a way to control AO intensity as well. Currently AO is completely unaffected by `intensity`. It would be very cool to have the ability to control lighting and AO intensity independently, so having something like a `bounce intensity` and `AO intensity` pair of settings. As for performance: I haven't looked at it at all yet, I wanted to do visual comparisons first. I haven't used SSIL in my projects much if at all (I use SSAO though), so I'm probably not the most experienced on SSIL usage. But I thought that providing some comparisons would be useful to the PR, hence this post.

Yes the separated intensities are intentional, but the AO strength is currently hardcoded to 0.5, which may be why some occlusion is weak. I have to add it as an actual parameter first, and I was thinking of possibly making a way to also increase the actual intensity (such as a pow() function on the ao) as the strength just mixes how much it effects the image.

Performance benchmarks for PR SSIL. Setup: AMD RX 570 4GB, RADV 25.2.8, 1920x1080 fullscreen. Scene: same scene (Bistro) and view from my previous tests, with a spinning 1m cube, and everything except SSIL disabled. SSIL was used in mode `both`. ## Results
Raw benchmark data Normal rejection enabled: | | 1.0m | 2.0m | 3.0m | 4.0m | 6.0m | 8.0m | 16.0m | |----------|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:| | very low | 10.00ms | 11.40ms | 12.35ms | 12.90ms | 13.20ms | 13.16ms | 12.60ms | | low | 9.90ms | 11.40ms | 12.35ms | 12.90ms | 13.20ms | 13.16ms | 12.60ms | | medium | 11.45ms | 12.50ms | 13.80ms | 14.80ms | 16.13ms | 16.80ms | 16.80ms | | high | 13.35ms | 14.33ms | 15.38ms | 16.80ms | 19.23ms | 20.90ms | 23.00ms | | ultra | 17.10ms | 18.70ms | 19.70ms | 21.25ms | 25.00ms | 28.18ms | 33.90ms | Normal rejection disabled: | | 1.0m | 2.0m | 3.0m | 4.0m | 6.0m | 8.0m | 16.0m | |----------|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:| | very low | 9.30ms | 10.36ms | 11.15ms | 11.55ms | 11.95ms | 11.90ms | 11.43ms | | low | 9.30ms | 10.36ms | 11.15ms | 11.55ms | 11.90ms | 11.90ms | 11.43ms | | medium | 11.05ms | 11.60ms | 12.42ms | 13.20ms | 14.29ms | 14.85ms | 15.00ms | | high | 12.72ms | 13.60ms | 14.10ms | 14.80ms | 16.53ms | 17.86ms | 19.80ms | | ultra | 16.00ms | 17.70ms | 18.60ms | 19.23ms | 21.10ms | 23.54ms | 29.00ms |
Note: - `reference` refers to the empty scene, with no GI or any post processing enabled in the world environment. It's the baseline scene render time. - `VoxelGI 256` refers to the render time of `reference`, with an added 256 subdivision fully static 6-cone VoxelGI rendering at full resolution. This is intended to provide some context for the new SSIL's performance against other existing effects. - `low` and `very low` have pretty much identical test results, so they overlap. Overall, at least on my card, the performance for what I would consider an acceptable quality level (medium/high with 2m radius) seems to be around that or somewhat worse than a 256 VoxelGI.

Ok, I believe for the most part I've fixed some issues regarding this. A lot of it seems to just be inherit limitations sadly, such as crazy effects if you boost intensity beyond 4. But, at high, 2.0 intensity, 16 radius, i now get this with zero ambient contribution:

> And I am curious as to where the added performance cost is coming from with higher radius... As I understand it, the algorithm has a fixed number of texture reads for all radiuses. Considering that on my GPU the bottleneck seems to be memory bandwidth (improving occupancy *worsens* performance), then my best bet is on less cache hits happening from texture reads, since they're more spread apart. The RX570 has 16kb of L1 per CU (total 512kb) and 2MB of L2 cache, then it's off to VRAM. A 1920x1080 32-bit depth buffer is ~8MB, it's not fitting into the caches. Then you put in the albedo and the normals and it gets worse. There's a really neat diagram of AMD GPUs' memory hierarchy in the [official AMD GCN3 ISA docs](https://docs.amd.com/v/u/en-US/gcn3-instruction-set-architecture), page 21: Optimizing bandwidth usage at hardware level is hard though. It's probably better not to go into that rabbit hole :| ...Not yet at least :P

I wanted to circle back on this as I was thinking about it, and issues have been arising with how the AO logic flows, which leads me to believe that other contributors later on may have trouble if it is structured this way. I feel some of this should be split into different PRs.

While working on this PR further, I noticed in `scene_forward_clustered.glsl` that there is a dedicated ao parameter used for direct lighting & SSAO. I was going to use this parameter to also add the AO from SSIL onto the direct light, but that would involve overwriting the SSAO. I could get around that by adding a separate ao parameter that works the same and also affects direct light, but it all seems a bit roundabout, and you'd have to pile on another parameter for a direct light effect on the GTAO.

@Image-unavailable had said in their testing of this PR that the GTAO shouldn't be viewed as a replacement to SSAO and rather should be used in conjunction with it. That would raise performance concerns, and I believe that reasoning came from the fact that the PR at the time lacked adjustable AO params. I had the effect hardcoded at 0.5 which led to the use of SSAO to make up for it. GTAO/GTAOVB is a great contender to replace SSAO in the same way #113304 handles it. However that seems like a decision best for a broader discussion.

This PR's GTAOVB implementation is worth noting as it flows with the rest of the SSILVB with little added overhead due to sharing most of the logic with the SSILVB. But, the AO work seems like a decision for a different PR/discussion. This PR should focus on the SSIL rewrite since that's its main purpose, hence the title. In the current state of SSAO and SSIL being in different files, it would be convoluted and confusing to have AO logic flowing into the SSIL file, and with the way I handle this, that is needed to maintain its good performance. But with the scope of this PR I don't see it logical to go about that since that branches into larger overarching structures and issues.

Of course I'd like to know what you guys think about all of this before going forward with changes for this to the code I have, but thought it was worth bringing up.

How difficult is it to "extract"/decouple GTAOVB from SSILVB without losing performance? I mean, replacing SSILType with SSAOType

> How difficult is it to "extract"/decouple GTAOVB from SSILVB without losing performance? I mean, replacing SSILType with SSAOType

I assume it wouldn't be that difficult, you just generate the GTAOVB in the SSILVB file if an ssaotype parameter (which would basically just be ssiltype but renamed and moved to the ssao section in project settings) is set to GTAOVB. But as I said before that would probably feel quite convuluted and be confusing to future contributors which is the main reason I'd like to steer away from doing that.

Also, of note is that generating the GTAOVB on top of the SSILVB isn't actually free, the reason it seems that way right now is because setting the SSILType parameter doesn't actually stop any logic from running, so if the type is "ao" then all the indirect lighting logic is still running, it just isn't contributing to the final image, and vice versa. SDFGI shouldn't be used as a reference for realistic lighting, as it's only an approximation. Same goes for VoxelGI. If you want a reference for how photorealistic lighting looks in a scene, you should do a render with a pure raytracer like Blender's Cycles: 16k samples, no denoiser, full GI preset (32 bounces), 0.001 noise threshold, no direct/indirect clamp, all caustics on, no glossy filtering. This is maybe even overkill, and it takes a while to render even simple scenes, but it's what should give the most true-to-life results.
